paras: The death of Wilson Calder was the death of a Black man on Edisto Island, South Carolina, on July 3, 1881, two days after he fought two white brothers, Marlon and Harry Seabrook. Black residents held that the fight killed him, a doctor found no marks of violence, and the dispute halted the inquest and left the body unburied about a week.
According to the constable, the brothers, sons of Edward W. Seabrook, "got into a difficulty" with Calder on July 1 over language he used toward them.

Marlon Seabrook struck Calder with his fist, a "regular fisticuff" followed, and Harry Seabrook picked up a brick but did not use it. Calder ploughed all the next day without complaint, the constable said, and died the following morning after eating "a potful of parboiled hominy."

Seabrook Whaley organized a coroner's jury of seven white and five Black men, which heard ten witnesses. Dr. Murray testified that the body bore no marks of violence except a burn between the shoulders, attributed to a fall into a fire during an epileptic fit. The Black jurors demanded a verdict of willful murder and an autopsy, which the deputy coroner refused, and the jury dispersed without a verdict.

The body lay in the open air until, by July 11, the coroner had empanelled a new jury, an autopsy had been held, and Calder was buried. The dispatch warned that anyone interfering with the new inquest would be arrested; no verdict or charge against the Seabrooks appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News headlined its account "MULISH JURORS" and called the Black residents' belief "not probable," though it reported that many whites blamed the deputy coroner for the excitement. A Charleston dispatch in the same paper reported the autopsy and burial, and the Southern Christian Advocate gave the affair one line, blaming the "wild excitement of the negro inhabitants" for stopping the inquest.

The cause of death remained disputed: the Black jurors blamed the fight, the constable and Dr. Murray other causes, and the Southern Christian Advocate said Calder "had been burned to death in his cabin."

reader.title: Death of Wilson Calder
bases: The only account of the violence is a fistfight in which two named white brothers struck Wilson Calder after he 'used such language towards them', followed by a death whose cause was disputed at the inquest; no mob or band is reported (A1).

Black jurors and residents held that Calder died of injuries from the Seabrook fight, while the constable, the examining doctor and the Savannah correspondent denied it (A1); a third report says he was 'burned to death in his cabin' and does not mention a fight (A3).

accounts.label: Constable's account (via Savannah correspondent)
accounts.gist: Calder's language provoked Marlon Seabrook to strike him; after the fistfight Calder worked all the next day, ate 'a potful of parboiled hominy' that night and died the next morning.

accounts.label: Dr. Murray's testimony
accounts.gist: No marks of violence except a bad burn between the shoulders, which it was 'proved' Calder got by falling into a fire during an epileptic fit.

accounts.label: Black jurors and residents
accounts.gist: Calder was killed by Seabrook in the fight; they demanded a verdict of willful murder and an autopsy to find internal injuries.

accounts.label: Southern Christian Advocate brief
accounts.gist: A Black man 'had been burned to death in his cabin'; Black residents' excitement prevented the coroner's inquest.

framing.detail: Headlined 'MULISH JURORS'; called the Black jurors' belief 'not probable' and said 'of course' the jury refused a murder verdict, while reporting that many whites blamed the deputy coroner for the excitement.
Short Charleston dispatch on the new inquest and autopsy, noting the body had been 'allowed by the negroes to remain above ground for a week' and warning of arrests.
One-line item in a news column, framed around the 'wild excitement of the negro inhabitants' stopping the inquest.
